item.title: Obernolte-Trahan artificial intelligence bill introduced in House
item.description:
# Obernolte-Trahan artificial intelligence bill introduced in House 07/23/2026 11:40 AM EDT
Two key House lawmakers introduced an [artificial intelligence bill](https://legislation.politicopro.com/bill/US_119_HR_9925) Thursday that would preempt some state AI laws and give the government the ability to restrict deployment of models determined to pose catastrophic risks, according to three people familiar with the proposal.
Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.), follows a [discussion draft unveiled last month](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/06/04/obernolte-trahan-ai-bill-lands-on-the-hill-00949920).
It represents the latest bipartisan attempt to establish a federal framework for AI governance after Congress has repeatedly failed to advance broad legislation.
But it includes specific carveouts to allow state laws to regulate the deployment of AI and child safety, among others.
Bill cosponsors include Reps. Scott Peters (D-Calif.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Suhas Subramanyan (D-Va.) and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.).

item.title: Manhattan University Announces Minor in Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
# Manhattan University Announces Minor in Artificial Intelligence Starting Fall 2026, Manhattan University is launching a new minor program in Artificial Intelligence.
Image
![AI or Artificial intelligence concept. Businessman using computer use ai to help business and used in daily life, Digital Transformation, Internet of Things, Artificial intelligence brain,](https://manhattan.edu/sites/default/files/styles/4_3_327w/public/media/2026-07/ai-minor-3000x2000.jpg?h=c6980913&itok=lYbPpHEH)
RIVERDALE, N.Y. — Manhattan University will launch a [minor in artificial intelligence](https://manhattan.edu/academics/programs/ai-minor) in fall 2026, giving students across every discipline structured instruction in how intelligent systems work and how to apply them responsibly.
The new minor draws on the combined strengths of all three of the University's schools, the Kakos School of Arts and Sciences, the O'Malley School of Business and the School of Engineering, and builds on established programs in computer science, computer information systems, business analytics, and electrical and computer engineering.
"Artificial intelligence touches every discipline, and our students deserve more than a surface-level familiarity with it," said Bridget Chalk, Ph.D., provost of Manhattan University. "This minor gives students in any major, from business to engineering to the liberal arts, a genuine understanding of how AI works and how to use it responsibly in their fields."
Open to students in every major across the University, the minor was developed jointly by faculty in computer science, computer information systems, business analytics, accounting, law, and electrical, computer and mechanical engineering. It provides structured, interdisciplinary instruction in AI fundamentals: how intelligent systems work, what their limitations are and how to apply them responsibly.
Students choose from a core of upper-level courses in areas including machine learning, data mining, deep learning and generative AI, trustworthy AI, image processing, and AI applications in business and engineering design. Tailored pathways accommodate students with and without prior programming experience, ensuring the minor is both accessible and academically rigorous.
Consistent with the University's Lasallian mission, the minor also challenges students to weigh the ethical and societal implications of artificial intelligence, asking not only what intelligent systems can do, but what they should do.
For more information, visit manhattan.edu/AI.

item.title: Universities ask for $24.5 million to launch and maintain artificial intelligence system
item.description:
## Funding for artificial intelligence As the board plans to use artificial intelligence in its business and educational operations, it’s requesting $20 million in one-time funding to build out its AI technology system and $4.5 million in ongoing funding to maintain it.
The board approved a [new AI policy](https://public.onboardmeetings.com/Meeting/zLuYkXtbyNn5RXDOzWJc8xAlLnZUwLtRMTL1WF47V70A/ukFk4XIQFCrHLBTOxDywCtPncO32R4Ci6EzDejBxNi4A/ZBavYnBoyiBu9rj1Ypqp%2FpyxecQEKJsFkBoPR7GUtjQA/dnp6nurOQvgUAmkORjAuW8sWDgk6UaP7XUZpNHreSBsA/Agenda%20Document) at its Thursday meeting, and the board will launch a system-wide software this fall that supports several AI uses and future emerging technologies, said David Overby, interim system chief information officer.
[Board of Regents ‘leaning in’ to AI while planning to regulate its use at South Dakota universities](https://southdakotasearchlight.com/2026/05/23/board-regents-leaning-artificial-intelligence-regulate-use-south-dakota-universities/)
Board of Regents ‘leaning in’ to AI while planning to regulate its use at South Dakota universities • South Dakota Searchlight
[Board of Regents ‘leaning in’ to AI while planning to regulate its use at South Dakota universities](https://southdakotasearchlight.com/2026/05/23/board-regents-leaning-artificial-intelligence-regulate-use-south-dakota-universities/)
South Dakota universities are “leaning in” to artificial intelligence, state Board of Regents President Jeff Partridge said at a Wednesday meeting in Custer. The system that oversees the state’s public universities plans to formulate regulations for AI use throughout 2026 and 2027, focusing on how the technology should be governed; how to teach students, faculty … [Continue reading Board of Regents ‘leaning in’ to AI while planning to regulate its use at South Dakota universities](https://southdakotasearchlight.com/2026/05/23/board-regents-leaning-artificial-intelligence-regulate-use-south-dakota-universities/)
“This policy provides a way to enable AI innovation across the regental system while maintaining clear boundaries around data protection, security, oversight and accountability,” Overby said. “It supports responsible adoption without treating AI as unmanaged or standalone technology.”
The board also approved four AI academic programs on Thursday: a doctorate in AI at Dakota State University and bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees in artificial intelligence engineering at South Dakota State University.
The $4.5 million additional ongoing request would be used to maintain the AI infrastructure by replacing aging equipment, building out technology infrastructure and funding cybersecurity needs. South Dakota State University President Barry Dunn said AI is increasingly used at universities across the nation.
“This opportunity is not simply to make AI tools available, but to use AI responsibly to improve service efficiency, accessibility and decision-making across the regental system,” Dunn said.
